exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Order CSF 14‑3‑3 protein; a positive result supports Creutzfeldt‑Jakob disease, guiding supportive care only.

A patient with longstanding TB develops nephrotic‑range proteinuria – which investigation confirms the suspected complication? — Perform kidney biopsy with Congo red stain; apple‑green birefringence confirms AA amyloidosis.
How does the pathophysiology of sickle‑cell disease illustrate protein misfolding? — Hemoglobin S polymerises under deoxygenation, behaving like a misfolded protein that damages vasculature.

In a low‑resource setting without electrophoresis, how would you suspect AL amyloidosis? — Look for unexplained macroglossia, periorbital purpura, and heart failure; treat empirically with plasma‑cell‑directed therapy if available.
Why is colchicine used in secondary amyloidosis and when should it be avoided? — It reduces serum amyloid A production; avoid in severe renal impairment due to toxicity.

What distinguishes prion disease from viral encephalitis on examination? — Prion disease shows myoclonus and lack of CSF pleocytosis, whereas viral encephalitis has fever, neck stiffness and CSF inflammation.
ai.title: Protein Misfolding Disorders
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Protein misfolding leads to toxic aggregates that cause organ dysfunction. Recognise common diseases, their clinical clues, and limited investigations in low‑resource settings.

b: Misfolded proteins can be inherited (e.g., cystic fibrosis) or acquired (e.g., prion disease).
Aggregates trigger inflammation, oxidative stress and cell death.
sections.p: Proteins must fold into precise three‑dimensional shapes to function. Errors in folding produce insoluble aggregates that damage cells, especially in the brain, liver and kidneys.

b: Amyloid: β‑pleated sheet structure, Congo red‑positive, apple‑green birefringence.
Prion: infectious protein that induces normal prion conversion.
sections.p: The cell uses chaperones and the ubiquitin‑proteasome system to prevent misfolding. When overwhelmed, aggregates accumulate as amyloid or inclusion bodies.

b: Rapidly progressive dementia → suspect prion disease.
Nephrotic syndrome with low‑grade fever → consider secondary amyloidosis.
sections.p: Common misfolding diseases in low‑resource settings include HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder (protein aggregation), sickle‑cell disease (hemoglobin polymerisation), and endemic amyloidosis from chronic infections.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical pattern, basic labs (proteinuria, liver enzymes) and response to empirical therapy.

t.b: Helps differentiate Creutzfeldt‑Jakob disease from other encephalopathies; positive supports prion disease.
Detects monoclonal light‑chain spikes; abnormal pattern suggests AL amyloidosis.

t.a: Kidney biopsy with Congo red stain
t.b: Confirms amyloid deposition; apple‑green birefringence under polarized light.
Identifies inherited mutations (e.g., transthyretin, cystic fibrosis); not essential for acute management.

b: Prion disease: supportive care only; avoid invasive procedures that may spread infectivity.
AL amyloidosis: chemotherapy targeting plasma cells (e.g., melphalan) when available; otherwise focus on heart failure management.
Secondary amyloidosis: treat chronic infection (e.g., TB, HIV) and use colchicine if available.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, reduce aggregate load, and support organ function.

b: Viral encephalitis vs. prion disease – CSF pleocytosis present in infection, absent in prion.
Nephrotic syndrome from minimal change disease vs. amyloidosis – amyloid shows Congo red positivity.
sections.p: Differential diagnoses that mimic protein‑misfolding presentations.

b: Normal CSF protein does not exclude early prion disease.
Serum electrophoresis may be normal in early AL amyloidosis; tissue biopsy is definitive.
Rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus → think Creutzfeldt‑Jakob disease.
Proteinuria + low‑grade fever in TB endemic area → secondary AA amyloidosis.
Congo red‑positive deposits → amyloid, not fibrin or collagen.
